title: Anterior TMJ dislocation: lateral pterygoid holds the jaw open
vignette: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. He is now awake but unable to close his mouth, which remains fixed in an open position, and he has difficulty speaking and swallowing. Examination shows the mandible protruded and locked open, with a palpable depression just anterior to each tragus. Imaging confirms bilateral anterior temporomandibular joint dislocation, with the mandibular condyles displaced anterior to the articular eminences. Spasm/overactivity of which of the following muscles is most responsible for maintaining this patient's jaw in the dislocated position?

clues.text: unable to close his mouth, which remains fixed in an open position
clues.note: An open, locked jaw that cannot close is the hallmark of anterior TMJ dislocation - the condyle is stuck anterior to the articular eminence.
Protrusion + inability to close reflects the pull of the muscle that protracts and depresses the mandible (lateral pterygoid).

clues.text: condyles displaced anterior to the articular eminences
clues.note: Anterior displacement of the condyle past the articular eminence is exactly where the lateral pterygoid pulls it; spasm keeps it there.

whatMatters: After a seizure, a jaw locked open with the condyles displaced anterior to the articular eminence = anterior TMJ dislocation. The LATERAL PTERYGOID protrudes and depresses (opens) the mandible by pulling the condyle forward; its spasm holds the condyle anterior to the eminence, keeping the jaw dislocated open. Answer C.
strategy: Sort the muscles of mastication by action. Elevators (close the jaw): masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid. Depressor/protruder (opens, pulls condyle forward): lateral pterygoid ('Lateral Lowers'). A jaw stuck OPEN with anterior condylar displacement implicates the lateral pterygoid. Reject the elevators and the genioglossus (a tongue muscle).

eliminations.label: Masseter - jaw elevator (closes)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a powerful elevator of the mandible that closes the jaw. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it would help CLOSE the mouth; it doesn't pull the condyle anteriorly to lock the jaw open. ✅ Correct if: forceful jaw clenching/biting.

eliminations.label: Genioglossus - tongue protruder, not a jaw muscle (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an extrinsic tongue muscle (CN XII) that protrudes the tongue. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it moves the tongue, not the temporomandibular joint, and has no role in dislocating/holding the mandible. ✅ Correct if: tongue deviation/hypoglossal nerve questions.

eliminations.label: Medial pterygoid - elevator (closes), part of protrusion
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an elevator that (with the lateral pterygoid) assists protrusion. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: its predominant action is to ELEVATE/close the jaw, not to depress and hold it open anteriorly. ✅ Correct if: jaw elevation with a medially directed component.

eliminations.label: Temporalis - elevator + retractor (closes/pulls back)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: elevates and retracts the mandible. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it closes and RETRACTS the jaw - opposite of the anterior displacement seen here. ✅ Correct if: jaw closing/retraction (its posterior fibers retract the mandible).

reasoning: Post-seizure jaw locked open, condyles anterior to the articular eminence = anterior TMJ dislocation
Muscles of mastication: elevators = masseter/temporalis/medial pterygoid; the lateral pterygoid depresses and protrudes (pulls the condyle forward)
Lateral pterygoid spasm holds the condyle anterior to the eminence, maintaining the open dislocation
mechanism: The temporomandibular joint's condyle normally glides forward onto the articular eminence during mouth opening, pulled by the LATERAL (external) PTERYGOID - the one muscle of mastication that DEPRESSES (opens) and PROTRUDES the mandible ('Lateral Lowers'). In anterior TMJ dislocation, the condyle passes anterior to the articular eminence and cannot return; sustained lateral pterygoid contraction/spasm (as can be triggered by wide opening during a seizure, yawning, or dental procedures) holds it there, locking the jaw open. The other muscles of mastication - masseter, temporalis, and medial pterygoid - are jaw ELEVATORS (temporalis also retracts), all innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3); their action would close or retract the jaw, not maintain the anterior dislocation. Reduction requires pushing the mandible down and back to slip the condyle back behind the eminence. The genioglossus is a tongue muscle (CN XII) and is irrelevant to the TMJ.

difficulty.label: 📚 Pure knowledge gap
difficulty.message: First Aid Anatomy > muscles of mastication (CN V3): masseter/temporalis/medial pterygoid elevate; lateral pterygoid depresses + protrudes ('Lateral Lowers'); TMJ anterior dislocation.

difficulty.label: 🧭 Understanding the question
difficulty.message: A jaw stuck OPEN with anterior condylar displacement implicates the depressor/protruder = lateral pterygoid.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocabulary
difficulty.message: Unsure on lateral vs medial pterygoid, articular eminence, protrusion vs retraction, or CN V3 innervation? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🧲 Pulled by a distractor
difficulty.message: Masseter/temporalis/medial pterygoid CLOSE (temporalis retracts); genioglossus is a tongue muscle (CN XII) - none holds an anterior TMJ dislocation.

difficulty.label: ✍️ Something else
difficulty.message: Bank: lateral pterygoid opens/protrudes the jaw ('Lateral Lowers'); anterior TMJ dislocation = condyle anterior to articular eminence.

keywords.front: Only muscle of mastication that opens/protrudes the jaw
Jaw locked open, condyle anterior to eminence

keywords.back: Mandibular division of trigeminal nerve (CN V3)
Protrudes the tongue; hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)

memoryHook: 'Lateral Lowers' - the lateral pterygoid yanks the jaw forward and down; in spasm it locks a post-seizure jaw wide open.
